after.en: If the judge stands still while the generator trains hard, the generator puts every sample on the one spot the judge trusts most: the two pens merge and draw only one cluster. This is mode collapse; as soon as the judge reacts, they jump together to the other cluster. Let the judge keep up and the generator take small steps, and the pens settle on one cluster each, until the judge's accuracy is back to 50%.

t.en: Earlier, reconstruction error trained the encoder and decoder. Adversarial training uses a different signal: a discriminator tries to tell real and generated samples apart, and the generator improves its output using that judgement.

Another way to generate is to have two models spar: a generator draws fake samples and a judge decides which are real. The better the judge gets at telling, the more convincing the generator has to be. This is called a generative adversarial network (GAN), and the "faces of people who don't exist" you see online are drawn this way.

The real data on the bench is two clusters of points. The generator has two pens, each drawing in one spot. The judge is a curve D(x): the higher it is, the more the judge believes a point there is real.
The two sides train in turns. You decide how many steps the judge trains each round, how many the generator trains, and how far the generator moves with each step.

In this level both clusters must be drawn, leaving the judge only able to guess, with its accuracy back at one half. Before you start, think: what difference does it make which side trains more, and which moves faster?

brief.en: The generator has two pens and must draw two clusters of points just like the real data. Take turns training the judge and the generator until both clusters are covered and the judge can only guess.

hint.en: If the generator moves too far in one round, both pens rush together to the spot the judge trusts most right now.

text.en: Goals · all at once, 3 rounds in a row
